name: FWAG Kilkenny Farm Survey 2026
description:
Wandering along the public footpath that goes right past this shelterbelt, Phil went to see how things were coming along.

Clearly this is a site that needs a shelterbelt, the wind was intense for the entire survey, but that wind is making life difficult for the saplings. They are all bent over from consistent prevailing winds from the south west.

First, the survival rates. The shelterbelt is split in half by a track, so North and South were counted separately.

- North: 50 alive out of 52 counted = 96.15% survival
- South: 87 alive out of 101 counted = 86.13% survival
- Overall: 137 alive out of 153 counted = 89.54% survival
Although that’s an impressive survival rate, “alive” is not the only metric for success here. Many of these have been ringbarked by browsing deer, with 2 meters of growth on the main trunk killed off, turning the trees into shrubs as they regrow from the base. These will be stronger against drought and winds, and more resilient to deer, but we need to protect them enough they can start doing their job as a shelterbelt.

How have the deer managed to get past the guards? These are the standard recycled/recyclable deer guards we usually use: the Defender Tree Shelters. This location is so windy they are struggling. Worse, the team doing the planting unfortunately selected the wrong holes when sliding these guards onto the wooden stakes. The guards are universal and support many common wooden stake dimensions, but these are small stakes with big holes selected. The wind has rattled them around so aggressively that many of the guards have split, exposing trees large and small to deer who have taken their heads off, or eaten enough of the bark to kill off the main trunk. Switching to windproof “mesh” guards will be the solution here.

A maintenance day should be organised with the landowner to get this tidied up, damaged guards removed and recycled, and replaced where necessary with “photodegradable” windproof guards like Continental Fine Mesh Shelter.

description:
## Site tour with John Hodgson (Upper Duddon Landscape Recovery Volunteering and Engagement Manager)

- On the drive to the see the saplings planted by Protect Earth, we stopped to take a look at the conifer plantations thinned over the years. This management served a dual purpose: supporting natural regeneration among native trees long dwarfed by the conifer canopy, and managing the spread of Phytophthora ramorum through targeted larch felling. The felled larch is processed on-site and reused within one mile for local forest infrastructure, such as posts and fencing.
- Following years of planning, last year,  neighbouring farms came on board to form a lad cluster, expanding the landscapes recovery project (see map photo)
- Driving higher up, we gained a sweeping view of the area felled in 2014.
- The sheer scale of the felling is remarkable, and natural regeneration—oak, birch, and Scots pine—is already clearly visible across the landscape. (see our past photos for comparison)
- Some impressive statistics coming through with the research conducted on site - natural regeneration is yielding around 3,000 stems/ha, compared to a typical planting plan density of 1,200 stems/ha.
- From this view, John pointed out the plans for the planting of the neighbouring land parcels - sheep-free areas at high altitude that will be planted with shrubby willow, juniper and oaks and rowan to extend the tree line
- From this vantage point, John pointed out future planting plans across neighbouring land parcels—high-altitude, sheep-free areas destined for shrubby willow, juniper, oak, and rowan to extend the natural tree line.
- Further out, at the farthest section of Phil’s planting, John noted the dramatic impact of removing sheep (previously grazed by around 80–85 sheep). In just a few years without livestock, self-seeding trees and heather have surged back.
- Healthy hazels lined the ditches
- Deer browsing remains an ongoing challenge for untubed saplings and those self-seeded through natural regen. Two stalkers currently manage deer populations on site, with a third coming on board shortly.

- We passed lots of thriving heather and bilberry (stopping for a snack on the berries) and waded through head-height ferns, stopping top inspect the saplings planted in tubes within the bracken (tubes make locating and monitoring far easier here)

name: Low Fell Updates/Survey 2026
description:
## Site tour with Sally and Darren

It was a good 10-minute walk from the nearest layby, through narrow paths and ascending into the bracken before we reached the first area of planted land. Standing and looking over the ascending fell—an area where 150,000 trees were planted (10,000 of which were Protect Earth)—the realisation that this was no mean feat kicked in.

Low Fell would have been a temperate rainforest before becoming part of the lead mining industry 1,500 years ago. By 200 years ago, it was known to be a sheep farm.

As we were ascending, you could already see the impact of removing the grazing sheep from this land: a spate of self-seeded cherry trees were thriving above the bracken canopy.

As you adjusted your eyes to the bracken, you began to see just how many trees have already surpassed the canopy height—especially the silver birches, rowan, and some oak. Darren pointed out that they are doing particularly well when clustered together due to their mycorrhizal networks supporting each other’s growth.

We had to ascend with care, navigating lost trails because hidden under all this dense bracken were thousands of saplings yet to come up over the canopy. In two years, this site will look very different.

Sally explained her reverence for the bracken. Sally and Darren chose not to plant with tree guards—partly due to the cost and difficulty of bringing materials to this remote site, but also because they didn't want to bring plastic onto the land, which creates a visible dissonance with the green landscape. Initially criticised for their decision under the assumption that it would be to the detriment of the new trees, Sally and Darren began to see just how supportive the bracken actually was.

Firstly, it acts as shade, protecting the establishing saplings from the heat of the summer sun.

It also creates a physical barrier around the trees, deterring deer from entering the dense vegetation.

When the bracken dies back in autumn, it creates a natural mulch, and Sally and Darren have begun noticing second growth spurts in the saplings by October. Sally noted that you especially see this with the oaks, shown off by their red autumnal leaves.

We ascended about two-thirds of the way up, looking towards the more resilient montane species planted near the peak of the fell.

Sally and Darren have a close relationship with the landowners managing the land and riparian edges beneath the fell. Together, they have established a thriving, species-rich nature corridor, and they have noticed swallows and migratory swifts coming further inland since the planting began.

Looking across the valley, you could see the location of the first Christian outpost established here in 300 AD. In the field below, we could see a different tree plantation; its white plastic tube guards were uniformly arranged like a military cemetery, a stark contrast to the dense green fell, where many saplings are still hiding in the wildness.

I was excited to learn that Sally and Darren have just acquired their fourth site in the Lakes with their CIC. We are hoping to support them with further trees!

name: Highchurch Survey 2026
description:
Date of survey

: 29 September 2026

Photos:

Google photos link - let me know if you need some context for each of them:

https://photos.app.goo.gl/mktfSMwYzeqK2LHr7

Overall state of the site

Mixed picture: the heavy clay and south-facing slope make establishment difficult and recent weather extremes have hit it hard. In dry spells the clay cracks open around planting holes and exposes roots. Most, if not all, of the infill planted at the start of this year was lost to the summer drought. The established trees are in better shape, with roughly two-thirds of those surveyed alive. Several species are doing very well and some areas are thriving while others struggle.

Survival rate

I walked a transect through two sections from one end to the other, recording roughly two trees either side of me as thriving, surviving or dead. I dictated as I went and collated the results afterwards. Viweing the site as a clock face with North at 12, I covered the 9–11 o'clock and 3–6 o’clock sections. The thin strip at the top was not counted, but it is small enough that it is unlikely to change the overall picture.

The 9–11 o’clock strip had 115 of 160 trees alive (72%). The 3–6 o’clock strip had 86 of 137 alive (63%). Across both strips, 201 of 297 trees were alive (68%).

Most dead trees could not be identified - they are most likely this year’s restock, which the docs show as oak, hornbeam, hawthorn and hazel. Because of this, the per-species figures only reflect surviving trees.

Strongest performers

: Italian alder (almost all thriving), aspen, wild cherry, poplar and field maple.

Doing OK:

Field maple, silver birch, hazel and sessile oak survives almost everywhere but tends to be steady rather than vigorous. Hawthorn also did well.

Struggling:

Hornbeam is the weakest: most are alive, but only one was thriving. Small-leaved lime were in small numbers, doing OK in the lower sections where they had survived.

Survival rate comments

The top of the field, between about 1 and 3 o’clock at the very edges, has always been the hardest area and continues to struggle. Elsewhere there are better and worse patches with no obvious pattern. The bottom of the field has done well. It gets very wet in winter, which may help it hold moisture through summer.

Visible issues

There is mildew on field maple, very likely the common powdery mildew of field maple, which is rarely serious at this time of year. There is also probable spot on aspen. I saw no significant pest problems. The main pressures are drought, temperature swings and the clay.

Most of the alder on site is Italian alder (heart-shaped glossy leaves and large cones). Every planting order was for common alder, so this looks like a mis-supply. Italian alder isn’t a typical native woodland tree and may need active control as the site develops. It is however an amazing nurse species, as it fixes nitrogen, copes with both dry and heavy soils, and is currently the best performer on site. As a mid to long-term plan, if one doesn’t already exist, we should keep it as a nurse crop and then thin or coppice it once the native canopy is established.

The oak on the original order and this year’s restock was sessile oak, while the design said pedunculate oak. Forest Research says sessile oak prefers light, well-drained soils and is not suited to compacted or wet soils, whereas pedunculate oak prefers heavy, moist soils, which might explain the slow uptake? We should consider pendunculate for any restock here.

https://www.forestresearch.gov.uk/tools-and-resources/tree-species-database/131560-sessile-oak-sok/

https://www.forestresearch.gov.uk/tools-and-resources/tree-species-database/131559-pedunculate-oak-pok-2

Tree health

Overall health is mixed. David has been concerned about wind exposure, but I only noticed a couple of trees misshapen by wind.

The bigger issue is that guards and canes are now harming some of the more established trees. Canes are rubbing stems in many places. Guards on larger trees are collecting debris, which breaks down into a permanently wet layer at the base of the trunk and in some cases the trees are rooting into it. Where canes have been knocked about by the wind, they’ve also opened up holes at the base that likely help the roots dry out.

Wherever I found these problems, I removed the guard and cane after checking the tree was stable enough to stand on its own. I removed around 5 - 10% of guards. The canes provide very little support and mostly just hold the guards in place. Guard and cane removal should be part of future maintenance on this site.

Restocking considerations

I’d recommend either leaving the 1-3 o’clock top corner to develop naturally rather than restocking it again and losing them all or considering species that might cope better there.

There are gaps elsewhere that need filling, but I think it’s worth rethinking our approach on clay sites rather than repeating the same mix. Soil additives such as gypsum, could in theory help, but it would have to be dug into the clay and isn’t realistic at this scale. Adding compost to planting holes apparently risks creating a “bathtub” that waterlogs roots in winter. Surface mulch around new stock is a better option: it holds moisture and reduces cracking at the surface. We've been doing this, but maybe it needs more regular replacement?

Two practical changes could shift the balance though:

1. Earlier planting in Nov/Dec, so roots keep growing through winter whenever the soil is above about 4-5°C. Late-winter planting may be leaving them reliant on very few new roots just as the clay starts to dry.2. Cell-grown stock instead of bare-root whips amy establish better on dry, heavy sites.Using species that are currently thriving would also help, but would reduce diversity. They need to cope with both drought and very wet years. In addition, adding pedunculate oak, instead of sessile oak, wild service tree, rowan and goat willow - all in the original design but never planted and all three suit this site. Crab apple and spindle would add more robustness and diversity and planting guelder rose and dogwood at the wetter bottom end. Hornbeam may do better if planted further down the road, under the shelter of the nurse trees.Controversial suggestion, I think it’s worth considering whether future restocks need guards at all - the deer fence is holding and there is little sign of rabbit browsing. Planting without guards would save cost and avoid the problems now affecting established trees.It would also help to record and mark the species in each restock. Most of this year’s dead trees couldn’t be evaluated because they couldn’t be identified.Additional observationsGround flora diversity is low, which is expected after agricultural use and may take time to recover. Buttercups are scattered throughout and dock is establishing. There is some ragwort and common fleabane, which is typical in wet heavy clay.Birds on site: red kites, kestrels and buzzards over the field, yellowhammers nearby, wren, robin and long-tailed tits in the hedges. There was a varied and interesting range of spiders, including a four-spot orb weaver and plenty of shield bugs. I saw almost no grasshoppers or beetles. David has two beehives and has also seen hare in the field.Natural regeneration is coming in from the edges, especially around the standalone oak at about 5 o’clock, with a lot of young oak seedlings growing well. Hazel and other species are also regenerating across the field. None of the natural regen I saw showed any browsing damage, including unguarded regen right next to guarded trees. The deer fence is working well and browsing pressure looks low. I saw only one tree with light browsing and one exposed root that had been chewed by small rodents.Two field elms, which look like they were planted separately, are doing extremely well - amazing bark!This site would really benefit from putting in two or three raptor perches, which are simple posts with a crossbar, spread around the field. They would give kestrels, owls and other birds of prey hunting points, help keep vole numbers down and support a healthier food web. Barn owl or kestrel boxes would be a good additional step if David wanted to fund and put them up or if a local nature org wanted to get involved.Website update comment: (is this a good enough length?)At High Church Farm, the established trees are holding on well after a tough summer on heavy clay. Alder, poplar, wild cherry, oak and field maple are leading the way. The deer fence is doing its job, kestrels and buzzards are hunting over the field and we’re adapting our approach to this tricky site for future planting.

## Field Observations

This site visit was relatively short and consisted mostly of noting down Darren's advice and accepting his gifted tools while being transported around the site in his Kubota. He was a force of nature and very gracious, but seemed eager to finish up the visit, and politely declined me making a precise survival count, pointing out that the site's survival rates are in line with report he previously sent in, and that things are progressing well. After touring the site with him, I agree.

Darren reports the following animals on-site:

- Kite
- Buzzard
- Roe deer
- Muntjac deer
## Survival Rates

The site is in overall excellent condition. The trees in 1a were planted after ~1 year of growth are very large, healthy, and well-established. The trees in 1b are much smaller, which Darren attributes to their being planted at a younger age (as whips) with less robust roots. Both areas have survival rates over 90%, and both appear healthy and well-cared-for.

1a: 99% survival

1b: 93% survival

Meadow:

Failed to support wildflowers even after being re-sown a second time with a rattle-heavy seed mix.

All other planting areas (for example, a small patch of oak planted on a slope by the house, and a couple of rows of saplings planted along a pathway):

99% survival

## Comments

Darren has found great success with mesh sapling guards; they seem to reduce the rate at which grass smothers the saplings, contributing to higher survival with less management.

On trees with standard guards made of coiled strips of solid translucent plastic, Darren reports that grass will often invade the space between the sapling and the guard's inner walls, growing rapidly up towards the top of the guard, wrapping their blades closely around the bark of saplings, and effectively smothering them to death, presumably through a combination of damp, elevated temperature, and blocking light from reaching the sapling through both the guard's translucent walls and open top. Darren lost several trees early on to this "sweating out", despite quite regular replacement of the weed-suppression matting around each sapling, and manually uncoiling each guard, ripping out any coiled grass, and replacing the guard. He reports much higher survival and less management need after switching to mesh guards.

The "bathtub lime" is also alive and doing well in a mesh guard. This was apparently kept hydrated by Phil in a hotel bathtub (?) on the night before it was planted. Very cute.

Deer are present on-site and have attacked saplings, but the problem is not severe and has not lead to concerning losses in our area. I only saw one sapling killed by deer in our planting areas.

Darren has found good success with using wood chip as a weed suppressant at the base of saplings, especially if it's been left outside for a year to grow fungal colonies prior to use.

## Landowner: Met with Darren Hudson

## Maintenance

Darren carried out:

- Mulching
- Weeding between trees
- Weeding within guards
- Straightening, replacing guards / stakes
Darren says he's perfectly happy with
the site's performance and feels able to
manage it himself

Oscar: Perhaps we could offer a flower meadow creation session for him, if we find any good ideas that might finally
help the flowers beat out the grass and get established?

Darren says he will probably want us to take some Oak saplings from him, either during this upcoming planting season or the next. He's planted them close together on a slope near his house and they are growing well.

If we can gather any more research into methods of transforming grass-dominated fields into wildflower meadows, I think Darren would be very receptive. He's now made two unsuccessful attempts, so might appreciate new ideas to help a third.

This site outside Llandrindod Wells in Mid Wales is doing amazingly well, with a 95% success rate. We used a mix of cell grown trees & ‘whips’ some of which have been suffocated by grasses (85% survival rate). The small leaved limes are doing well however the Silver Birch are not great the. The Oaks are doing extremely well with a 90% survival rate. Then Early pollinators crab apple etc  are 4yrs old now and up to 7ft.

The Wildflower meadow didn’t take although seeded well after ploughed and power harrowed there was little to no rain in the weeks ahead and the grass won, se we will be trying a yellow rattle heavy mix next time.

‘The meadow was a big disappointment, we had some flowers the first year, and then nothing the second year. Other meadow sowers experienced similar and I will try some yellow rattle plugs to see if we can break up the grass.’ Darren Hudson Landowner Powys

PANTPURLAIS Phase 1 - 99%, Phase 2 - 80%, Wildflower meadow 0%
2x fields of trees, Field A, planted in 2021 = 99% survival rate. Field B planted in 2022 = 80% survival rate.




The trees in field A (planted 2021) have a 99% survival rate, which is shockingly good. One theory is that these trees (which came from Thorne Trees) and were slightly older than usual. Many of the early pollinators (e.g: crab apple), are 4 years old now and up to 7ft already.

The trees in field B (planted 2022) have a 80% survival rate. This is mainly because we planted a load of silver birch, which were whips at best and got consumed by grass. The small leaved limes, which spent their first night in Wales, in a bath in the local hotel are doing well!

The meadow was a big disappointment, we had some flowers the first year, and then nothing the second year. It should be noted that other people experienced the same. Grass has won. The plan is to retry with yellow rattle plugs, to see if we can break up the grass and let other wildflowers come through.

name: Warleigh Scything Course 1
description:
Phil, Greg and Ania from Protect Earth were joined by neighbouring landowner Johnny and reserve volunteers and supporters Tom and Dougal to get to grips with the traditional art of scything. Led by Kai Lange, the group began with an introduction to the history of the craft, the ergonomics and engineering of the tools, and the vital skill of blade maintenance before heading out into the fields.

Faced with dry conditions, slopes, and hidden ants’ nests, Kai said that if the team could learn to scythe here, we’d be well set up for the any landscape. As part of Protect Earth’s commitment to minimising fossil fuel use from machinery, scything will be used to help establish, manage, and restore the nature reserve’s meadows. The cut grass will also double up as mulch for establishing saplings, helping lock in much-needed moisture in the dry years ahead.

Just as importantly, as Kai reminded us, in times gone by everyone in the village would have been out helping together in the fields. A great way to engage the body, our relationship to the land, and the community, scything offers a rewarding communal craft.

We will be holding a further session on the 5th of September which is now fully booked unless you can bring your own scythe.

description:
site update copy

We visited Stawley in September 2026, and immediately saw signs of saplings poking out from their guards. Approximately 95% of our planting has survived the hot weather, and there is plenty of natural regeneration from existing trees and shrubs on the site.
As we toured the area, we found evidence of birds including robins, chiffchaffs, and a sighting of a great spotted woodpecker. There was also signs of mice, and some larger dens that could be foxes or badgers.
This site is doing well overall, with multiple species of trees showing good growth and coping with the hot weather.

## Site Update Notes

The last time Angus visited this site was in December 2025 assisting Phil with maintenance of the sliver of this site which consists of the pre-existing conifer planting which is here.

My first impression was that I could immediately notice saplings poking out of the top of their guards throughout the site.

Fortunately the end of August finally gave way to some rain. Poking a finger into the top layer of soil about half an inch deep the soil is moist.

Hopefully the soil retains moisture going into September without another heatwave immediately drying it out.

There were several sapling where an animal had dug underneath the guard to try eating the tree, despite this it was still alive.

I heard robins, chiffchaffs and I had a sighting and spotted a great spotted woodpecker.

Naturally occurring, a bushy hazel and holly growing in the same spot, naturally forming a hedge habitat.

Abandoned mouse nests in the tree guards.

Animal den on site - fox? badger?

The wood piles created during the conifer management have begun to rot.

I photographed a section where the fence has been removed. I wonder it's is becoming a convenient entrance for deer, I noticed a concentration of animal droppings and disturbed ground near this spot.

I was happy to see a lot of regrowth from trees previously marked as dead.

I love sites where I struggle to find dead trees.

## Survival Rate Info

720 total counted (5% of 14,400), 681 alive = 95%

Consisting of:

Green section (Bullock Field Hill entrance, higher elevation) = 420 counted, 394 alive = 94%

Red section (lower elevation) = 300 sampled, 287 alive = 96%

Note: Green section sample is larger than red section sample because green section represents a larger proportion of the site.

## Survival Rate Comments

Area Performance: I noticed some trees on the peripheries more exposed to predation from deer, and mice nesting.

Tree Health: I noticed some diseased trees grouped together in the shade at the lowest elevation of the red section, perhaps numbering up to 30 trees.

Despite some trees showing stress from heat/drought, affected trees were still showing green leaves.

I was encouraged to see a lot of regrowth from trees previously marked as dead. (Survival rate was 94% last year so this may be contributing to the rates this year?)

Species Detail: Every species planted was well represented with a range of growth.

Issues with stakes/guards: no issues to report.

## Field Observations

I heard robins, chiffchaffs and I had a sighting of a great spotted woodpecker. I found alder leaf beetles. Abandoned mice nests in tree guards. Naturally regenerating hedge habitats at the lowest elevation of the  site.

Survey

# Beat up survey autumn 2025

7/9/2025, by @Andy Herd

Compartment names for the purpose of this report:

A. the small area to the east of the farm buildings - was 70 saplings, 100% loss 😭
B. the shelter belt 1st to be planted - immediately west of farm buildings, both sides of the telegraph pole - was 994 saplings
C. Small copse in between both shelter belts - 100 saplings, doing quite well compared to rest of site, estimate 30% loss
D. shelter belt furthest to the NW - 710 saplings


This project was only planted 1yr ago and is doing very badly. It is a very exposed site and has experienced significant winds. The land owner said that electric fencing is used when cows are in the field but this was not the case - cows were observed within the shelter belts which has definitely contributed to the losses. It’s very hard to determine which losses were weather vs cows.


## A) small area

100% loss 😭 (70  saplings lost)

## B) shelter belt 1

- Copse to telegraph line: 187 still standing, of which 50% surviving = 94 surviving
- Telegraph to road: 59 still standing, of which 80% surviving = 47 surviving. There was some evidence of mould inside a couple of tubes here.
Total surviving = 141 out of 994

there are no trees in this photo but the telegraph pole delineates two compartments of the shelter belt. Below here is the smaller compartment to the south of the telegraph line.

## C) copse

We planted 100 trees here and they’re relatively sheltered. Only one or two cow pats in this compartment. 70% survival rate = 70 remaining out of 100

## D) shelter belt 2

There are approximately 90 saplings still standing. Of these still standing, I sampled two groups of 10:

- One group had 50% survival rate (west end)
- Another group had 90% survival rate (east end)
Averaging to ~70%, estimated 65 saplings surviving out of 710

a mother and calves standing within our shelter belt


## Conclusions

Total surviving:

A) 0
B) 141
C) 70
D) 65

Total 276 out of 1874 = 15% (i.e. 85% losses)

Recommend we don’t replant any until permanent livestock fencing is in place around each compartment. It’s also worth considering if we can make any changes to make our saplings more resistant to wind damage.

name: Nannerch Survey 2025
description:
The north west areas were planted on the first day of our volunteer planting, and had the best survival rate by far. Protected by trees on two sides, and from a hill on another, they were all standing upright and doing brilliantly. The volunteers who planted it all cared so much about the planting that they even came back to help with the surveying, so this might a good sign that motivated caring volunteers can absolutely nail it compared to unmotivated bad contractors.

The eastern field is bad. The survival rates are low all over, and whilst we forgot to get the number for the south east corner, the survival rate is not good. Slightly better on the top half of the field, but any maintenance activities should be focused on this field to begin with.

There was no sign of deer damage, or anything eating them, just a lot of dead trees.

I’m putting this one down to poor contractors. Some were known to be problematic, and where they had been planting there would be 10% alive. Then next to that, one of the better ones would have been planting and the rate would be much higher.

Some photos were taken that show you a sea of orange crosses.

We did a two-leveled system here, with a dot being “could maybe possibly be alright” and a cross being “super definitely dead”, so we can start by replacing the crosses and leave the dots alone to see if they come back. Colors were orange and pink, no meaning between them, just ran out of orange paint.

Recommendations

- Replanting some in the east field.
- Spraying grass in Spring.
- Take ~200 stakes and ~100 guards for each thousand trees replacing, they were all falling apart and these guards dont come off nicely.
- Take staplers and a lot of staples.

Cycling back to this beautiful farm from Newcastle was a real treat. A rail trail the whole way, late August, everyone having a nice time on bikes. At the end, a steep uphill ride and to be honest a fairly prolonged push to get to the top.

The sheep had been fenced out of the two big triangles of planting that make up this shelter woodland. Bringing biodiversity into the farm whilst also protecting livestocking from the prevailing wind is a great idea, but for now the trees need protecting from the livestock. Thankfully the fence and the deer guards have lead to a solid 76% survival rate.

This is a little below our target of 80% (by year five), but it’s not worth going out for 4% just yet. We’ll see if the survival rate drops by next summer and get in there to replace losses if its down any further.

The bottom, near where the woodland is absolutely fine, it's just the middle bit.'Landowner very enthusiastic about the wildlife you have observed;'It is not uncommon, even in daylight, to see hedgehogs down there. So I picked him up and put him back with his family's nest, my husband keeps reminding me that if you've got hedgehogs, it means you've got a lot of wildlife. There's also a small wildlife pond in that woodland. In the last three weeks, we've seen three newts. There's always damselflies and dragonflies down there, swallows sitting on the fence and house Martens ready for a snack.There are a huge variety of grasses within the woodland, which we cut back in the autumn, none of them have been planted by ourselves. There were some wild orchids in there this year. There was blue chicory last year and butterflies are always butterflies down there at this time of year. name: River Roding Knotweed Spray
description:
The River Roding Trust are a dedicated collection of individuals taking on the almost overwhelming challenge of cleaning up the River Roding. This rare habitat is a tidal marsh, a unique ecosystem that would have covered much of London before it was all paved over. The team is fighting the tides of rubbish both in the river and on the banks, and fighting illegal sewage outflow to improve the water quality.

Japanese knotweed is a problem on the banks of the River Roding as it spreads rapidly. If left unchecked it would become an impossible task to get rid of it. Our job was to remove the invasive knotweed, so that the reedbeds can expand, helping to not only protect the ecosystem, but improve water quality in the river.

Removal needs to be carried out by qualified professionals, so no volunteers were involved in this event. It’s impossible to permanently remove Japanese Knotweed without the use of chemicals so we worked with the Environment Agency to decide on the safest and most environmentally-friendly chemicals to use in this area.

Amazingly, the weather stayed dry for the entire time so Phil and Mike were able to make excellent progress, even taking to a boat to reach some of the more inaccessible plants. They cleared around a hectare of river bank, which is the equivalent of one and a half football fields.

# Beat up survey autumn 2025

7/9/2025, by @Andy Herd

Compartment names for the purpose of this report:

A. the small area to the east of the farm buildings - was 70 saplings, 100% loss 😭
B. the shelter belt 1st to be planted - immediately west of farm buildings, both sides of the telegraph pole - was 994 saplings
C. Small copse in between both shelter belts - 100 saplings, doing quite well compared to rest of site, estimate 30% loss
D. shelter belt furthest to the NW - 710 saplings


This project was only planted 1yr ago and is doing very badly. It is a very exposed site and has experienced significant winds. The land owner said that electric fencing is used when cows are in the field but this was not the case - cows were observed within the shelter belts which has definitely contributed to the losses. It’s very hard to determine which losses were weather vs cows.


## A) small area

100% loss 😭 (70  saplings lost)

## B) shelter belt 1

- Copse to telegraph line: 187 still standing, of which 50% surviving = 94 surviving
- Telegraph to road: 59 still standing, of which 80% surviving = 47 surviving. There was some evidence of mould inside a couple of tubes here.
Total surviving = 141 out of 994

there are no trees in this photo but the telegraph pole delineates two compartments of the shelter belt. Below here is the smaller compartment to the south of the telegraph line.

## C) copse

We planted 100 trees here and they’re relatively sheltered. Only one or two cow pats in this compartment. 70% survival rate = 70 remaining out of 100

## D) shelter belt 2

There are approximately 90 saplings still standing. Of these still standing, I sampled two groups of 10:

- One group had 50% survival rate (west end)
- Another group had 90% survival rate (east end)
Averaging to ~70%, estimated 65 saplings surviving out of 710

a mother and calves standing within our shelter belt


## Conclusions

Total surviving:

A) 0
B) 141
C) 70
D) 65

Total 276 out of 1874 = 15% (i.e. 85% losses)

Recommend we don’t replant any until permanent livestock fencing is in place around each compartment. It’s also worth considering if we can make any changes to make our saplings more resistant to wind damage.

name: Highwood Clearing
description:
## Event Description

Come and help Protect Earth begin the decades long job of restoring High Wood to its former glory as a temperate rainforest. To start we’ll be clearing and thiinning some of the young conifers that were planted recently, to avoid having to wait 50 years before we can get on with the important work of restoring this woodland to benefit wildlife and carbon sequestration.

For decades High Wood has been managed as a commercial timber plantation, with Douglas Fir, Sitka Spruce, and Western Hemlock dominating the landscape. In order to give native species a chance to recolonise this ancient woodland we’ll need to make some space. That’s right, we’re going to be cutting down some trees! It might sound counter-intuative, but this is all folowing advice from our ecologist and forester, folks at the Woodland Trust, and with permission from the Forestry Commission.

So come along, bring your friends, and maybe pick yourself a Christmas tree in the process!

## Equiprment

- Thick work/gardening gloves (leather, thornproof, etc)
- Bow saws and Loppers if you have them (we have some)

description:
# Retrospective - Planting weekend 27/28 Feb 2021



What went well?

- Delegating a bunch of jobs like putting canes in the ground to volunteers worked well. I think we shouldn't be afraid to steal some people away from planting trees to do other random jobs in the future. Everyone wants to plant trees but there are lots of other important jobs to do.
- Baby Mjolnir is an awesome tool, I'm very proud
- Biodegradable spirals and lolly sticks was appreciated by many
- Many cute doggos
- I didn't fully realise how important the iphone app is until I was standing in a field with it, it's great that we have this

What could we do better?

- Ordering trees was a little stressful! I had no idea that there were so many things to think about. I think a big constraining factor was that nursery stocks were running low toward the end of the season. We want to have stock reserved way ahead of time
- Watering trees was difficult! We figured it out but it would be good to have a plan for next time
- Leaflet to tell people how to plant a tree
- Supervise volunteers for the first few times? Or perhaps an individual check of each tree that's been planted?
- Hand sanitiser and antibac spray was a nice idea but ended up being left in random places far away from people
- I didn't know about the positioning of trees and stuff, which species were going where and which species matched up with the varying types of protection. People asked me for questions but I didn't really know! Maybe next time we can have a meeting to make sure the core team can answer questions before people start arriving?
- Map with what goes in different areas updated after species replacements and laminated.
- We assumed that sunday afternoon would be as busy and productive as saturday morning and that was not the case. We ended up taking our foot off the gas and as a result we had trees left over
- Latin tree names took a while to decipher
- Wasn't a particularly good mix of species because volunteers went in a sequence and we didn't emphasise that they should be moving about
- we set the border really early but next time it would be good to add shrubs at the end
- Do everything once, do it right. Checklist of process to plant tree, get protection, take the photo and only then on to the next one

### Checklist for a tree

- roots are heeled in
- it has the appropriate protection
- the bottom of the spiral/tube is in the ground
- it has a label
- cable ties are tight
- the stake is far enough in the ground
- we have a photo of it

Random ideas

- Where we have big stakes let's just write the species on the stake instead of a lolly stick. Or maybe on the tube? (wouldn't work in the wet)
- Volunteers arrive at 10am. Team arrive at 8am, or afternoon/evening before.
- Get trees ordered a month before. Also make sure that the tree order has the name of a business if it's a business because one of our drivers drove back and forward a few time looking for "protect earth" instead of "howard court"
- Each of us supervise a small team - making sure they get the protection right, making sure they heel in the trees properly
- Have lots of tags already written out
- balls of string with labels on for when we split a bag of trees

Equipment wish list

- Dear Santa, I would quite like a John Deere Gator for lugging equipment and water around, and maybe an IBC to put in the back to fill it with water.
- Also a pump for moving water easily - turns out you can get an attachment for an electric drill (though from reading the reviews of another one, maybe we should think of something else "I don't think it is meant for professionals or any intensive use" and "I can get about 10 minutes (rough estimate) with a 2.5Ah battery and a Ryobi drill". Maybe something like this and a car battery?
- Couple of spools of 100-200m rope for marking out borders
- walkie talkies
- wellies not boots

The app

Overall it's great! It saved us so much time it's saved us vs any other method of loading these into airtable. Some random thoughts in loose order of priority:


It would be nice if we can minimise the amount of clicks and make the buttons a little bigger. All of the supervisor, site and stuff stay the same for all the trees in a session. The only thing that really needs to change is the species. Maybe it could be page 1 of the session is selecting those and then the only thing that changes on the next screens is 2) take a photo 3) check it looks ok with the lat long at the bottom 4) select species with big buttons then repeat from 2. A few times I found myself clicking another box instead of "save"


Enabling pinch to zoom on the photo preview would be nice! At the beginning the lighting was really challenging and it was hard to see if the photos were usable with the sun against the phone screen.


On the upload queue, sometimes I ended up taking a photo of the same tree twice and then I would realise and go into the upload queue to delete it.

- Can the upload work in the order of the oldest photo that was taken first? It's possible to start uploading but still keep taking photos. If an upload was happening at the time I ended up taking a duplicate photo then it would be instantly gone. I don't think that happened this time but it would be really easy to make that mistake and switching it to oldest first would minimise the risk.
- Could we add some sort of indicator to the upload queue to make it obvious which ones were taken first? I had a scattering of looooads of just 2 different species at the time so it took me a while to figure out that the top of the list was the most recent (maybe  X mins ago indicator?)

We often end up planting the same 3-4 species in close succession. Maybe at the top of the planting list we can have the species of the last 5 species (in the order of most recently selected at top), then a little


I ended up with pretty cold hands and wearing gloves. Even though they have conductive stuff on them for using phones they're still kinda clunky. Bigger buttons and less clicks would be great!


I crashed it a few times. I can't quite remember the sequence of events (sorry, there were a LOT of tree photos) but I think it happened when I hit cancel to go back, check a tree in the upload, then start a new session quickly. When I crashed it with an upload in progress there's no confirmation that no photos were lost from the upload at the point of crashing. If we ever lost that upload queue then we would be shafted!


—— under this marker are all fairly low priority compared to the feedback above it ——


I think the "notes" field might not end up in airtable? I added "probably" to a couple but they don't seem to have saved.


very minor niggles that are kinda inconsequential but maybe we could polish them?

- Some visibility over how much space the photos in the queue are using would be nice (Phil's phone ran out of space partway through and the app totally froze up)
- When you select a species (say Hazel for example) then click the species selector again it hovers over the next one down in the list (say Hawthorne, I can't remember) but in order to select hawthorne you have to move the selector away then move it back to hawthorne again

Some way of marking a mystery species would be nice. Maybe this doesn't get uploaded? Maybe we might want >1 photo of this one to chat about as a group later, then select one of the photos and tag it with the species and only then allow it to upload


Nice to have but no idea how complicated it would be to build and probably bottom of the list priority wise - it would be great if I could see a map of all the trees we've taken a photo of this site. This map would need to be zoomed in to the max. The main reason I suggest this is that even with marks on each tree it's easy to lose track of where we're up to, and this could get harder if >1 person is taking photos


EDD'S BRIEF THOUGHTS

Good stuff

- Lots of volunteers, we're spoilt with this and we need to make sure we use them efficiently
- We got a shit load of trees in the ground
- Weather was excellent - this could be a bad thing as if it was raining you could cut the volunteers down by half, and half their productivity again

Bad stuff

- Ordering timing - could have arranged it cheaper by using fewer suppliers and worrying less about species variety
- Stock control - we ordered too much so will mean we have to ship things to-and-from every time, and we couldn't plant everything we had
- I had some embarrassing encounters with people asking me tree questions, I should know more or we should aim to have an ecologist with us at each project

The planting area consists of 1ha shelterbelt. The site is improved grassland previously used for hay cutting, and slopes down westward towards the M6. Soils are wet, slightly acid, base-rich loamy and clayey.
The Woodland Trust will arrange for bare-rooted 40 60cm whips to be delivered to the site in advance along with tree shelters: 1925 trees and shrubs to be planted in PVC spiral shelters secured with canes, with 50 Scots Pine in staked 0.75m mesh guards, and 25 Holly in staked 0.75m tubex shrub shelters. No additional site preparation is required.

Shelterbelt planting design incorporates planting in rows, with shrub species planted on the outside, planting the larger species in weaving rows towards the centre of the belt, providing shelter and shade to wildlife using it as a corridor. The trees should be spaced at random with tight groups thinning to scattered shrub towards the edge of the woodland (the intention being to give the woodland a 'natural' look). Any open space within the planting area should be marked out by the landowner in advance. The planting density is 2000 trees per ha and they should be spaced accordingly.

description:
George from Lockhart Garrett sent the following report, after inspecting green/yellow areas and the existing woodland up to the right.

Tree Planting

For the areas marked in green as per you plan sent to me on 17th December, I would recommend the following species for planting;

1. Small-leaved lime (Tilia cordata) – It’s a great tree for invertebrates in spring as well as being quite climate change resilient. It is also growing well in the locality.
1. Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus) – Again, it is predicted to be a species for climate change resilience and aesthetically, a great tree.
1. Rowan (Sorbus aucuparia) – Given that the site is relatively exposed to the prevailing wind, a hardier species such as Rowan would suit. The berries it will produce will also be a good source of food for a number of bird species.
1. Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus) – This scored well on the Ecological Site Classification tool and is also seen growing well in the locality. It is reasonably fast growing and so good for carbon sequestration.
1. Wild Service Tree (Sorbus torminalis) – This also scored well on the Ecological site classification tool and is predicted to be resilient to climate change.
I haven’t included higher timber value broadleaves such as Oak or Beech given the exposure here. They would however, be good to include elsewhere on the site when it comes to planted the areas shaded in yellow on your plan.

After undertaking a search of the Historic Environment Record for the site, there are a couple of features that were noted – these are shown on the attached plan. The polygons outlined in blue (within the area shaded pink) are earthworks of four post medieval quarries (HER Ref: 39698) and the long green polygons are medieval and post medieval hollow ways (HER Ref: 39663). The Hollow Ways are currently used for vehicular access and I note that these are not planned to be planted and should remain as such however, I would recommend that the Quarry Earthworks should also remain unplanted.

Existing Woodland

Unfortunately, I don’t think that the existing woodland block is ancient woodland – they aren’t designated as such on MAGIC or the Forestry Commission map browser. There are 3 veteran Oak trees and 2 veteran Ash, the remaining woodland is characterised by old growth Hawthorn and Hazel. Looking back at historic maps to 1883 and aerial photographs from 1945, it appears that the majority of this wood was once patchy scrub which has since colonised the whole of the site and grown to what it is today.

There is some Ash here (approx. 10%) and I note that some have already been thinned around the large Oaks but it was difficult to tell how severely they had been impacted by Ash dieback. I would reassess the Ash in the summer to assess its condition and then fell if necessary. You should be cautious not cleanse the wood of Ash – targeting only those trees that require felling.

The hawthorn and hazel could be coppiced in places to structurally diversify the age class of these species in the stand however, coppice stool regrowth may need to be protected from deer (muntjac and Roe observed whilst on site).

There are some nice areas of open ground that should be retained but some gapping up of other areas of weak canopy could be undertaken. Small-leaved lime is growing well here and so could be planted along with oak and beech. However, other oak and beech that have been planted here have suffered from squirrel damage and so control of squirrels would be vital. Alder would grow well at the bottom of the slope, alongside the stream and pond.
